items.question_text:
A rigid support S holds two blocks in a vertical line using two inextensible wires, each 1 m long: the upper wire (negligible mass) hangs from S to a 2.9 kg block, and the lower wire (uniformly distributed mass 0.2 kg) hangs from that 2.9 kg block down to a 1.9 kg block below it. The entire system — blocks, wires and support — accelerates upward at 0.2 m/s². Taking g = 9.8 m/s², answer the following.
(a) Find the tension at the midpoint of the lower wire.
(b) Find the tension at the midpoint of the upper wire.
items.figure_description: A horizontal rigid support S at the top. From S, an upper (massless) wire hangs down to a 2.9 kg block. From that 2.9 kg block, a lower wire of mass 0.2 kg hangs down further to a 1.9 kg block at the bottom.

solution.approach: Cut the wire at each midpoint and apply Newton's second law to everything hanging below that cut, using the system's own upward acceleration.

steps.text: For the lower wire midpoint, the hanging mass below the cut is the 1.9 kg block plus half the lower wire's mass.
Apply Newton's second law to this hanging mass, which accelerates upward at 0.2 m/s² along with the whole system.
This gives the tension at the lower wire's midpoint.
For the upper wire midpoint, the upper wire is massless, so the mass below the cut is the 2.9 kg block plus the entire lower wire plus the 1.9 kg block.
Apply Newton's second law to this total hanging mass with the same upward acceleration.

common_mistakes.text: Using g alone instead of g + a gives 19.6 N and 49 N, ignoring that the whole system accelerates upward.
Forgetting to include half the lower wire's mass below the lower midpoint gives 1.9 × 10 = 19 N there instead of 20 N.

concept_tags: tension in a wire with distributed mass

items.question_text:
A 2 kg block rests on top of a 1 kg block, and the 1 kg block rests on a smooth (frictionless) horizontal surface. The friction coefficient between the two blocks is μ = 0.6. The 2 kg block is given an initial velocity of 3 m/s to the right, while the 1 kg block is given an initial velocity of 18 m/s to the left. Assume the lower block is long enough that the upper block never slides off it. Taking g = 10 m/s²,
(a) Work out the time at which the relative sliding between the two blocks stops.
(b) Work out the common velocity the two blocks share at that instant.
(c) Work out how far the 1 kg block and the 2 kg block each travel up to that instant.
items.figure_description: A 2 kg block sits on top of a 1 kg block; the 1 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal floor. The 2 kg (upper) block moves at 3 m/s to the right, and the 1 kg (lower) block moves at 18 m/s to the left.

solution.approach: Find the kinetic friction between the blocks from the top block's weight, get each block's constant acceleration, then find when their velocities become equal.

steps.text: The friction between the blocks depends on the normal force at their interface, which equals the weight of the top block alone.
The top block moves right relative to the bottom block, so friction acts left on the top block and right on the bottom block, by Newton's third law.
Write each block's velocity as a function of time and set them equal to find when relative motion stops.
Solve for the time and the common velocity.
Use the same time in each block's displacement equation to find how far each one moved.

final_answer.value: (a) t = 14/6 s ≈ 1.17 s; (b) common velocity = 4 m/s, in the direction the 1 kg block first moved; (c) the 2 kg block displaces 7/12 m ≈ 0.58 m and the 1 kg block displaces 77/6 m ≈ 12.83 m, both in the direction the 1 kg block first moved

common_mistakes.text: Using the combined weight of both blocks for friction instead of only the top block's weight gives friction = 18 N and a wrong stopping time of 7/9 s ≈ 0.78 s.
Taking the bottom block's initial speed as +18 m/s, the same direction as the top block, instead of −18 m/s, gives a negative, impossible time of −5/6 s.

items.question_text:
Three pulleys are connected one below another in a chain: the topmost is fixed to a ceiling, and two lighter pulleys hang below it in series, as shown in the figure.
(a) Using string-constraint equations, determine how the acceleration of point 2 is related to the acceleration of point 1.
items.figure_description: A large pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. Below it hang two smaller movable pulleys, P₂ (medium) and P₃ (small), one below the other, and at the bottom sits block 1 (a wide base block); block 2 hangs beside the chain. Three light strings are used. String S₁ passes over P₁: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end goes straight down to the axle of P₂. String S₂ passes over P₂: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end goes straight down to the axle of P₃. String S₃ passes over P₃: its left end goes straight down to block 1 and its right end hangs straight down to block 2. So three string ends are tied to block 1 (one from each pulley) and block 2 hangs from S₃ only. All strings are vertical; pulleys and strings are massless and frictionless. Measure the downward positions of block 1 (x₁), the axle of P₂ (x₃), the axle of P₃ (x₄) and block 2 (x₂) from a fixed horizontal line through P₁; a₁ and a₂ are the accelerations of blocks 1 and 2.

solution.approach: Write the constant-length equation for each of the three strings in turn, then combine the three to connect point 1 and block 2 directly.

steps.text: The string over the top fixed pulley P₁ runs from block 1 to the axle of pulley P₂ (position x₃), so their distances from the reference line add to a constant.
The string S₂ over pulley P₂ (axle at x₃) runs from block 1 to the axle of pulley P₃ (at x₄), both measured relative to P₂'s own position.
The string S₃ over pulley P₃ (axle at x₄) runs from block 1 to block 2, both measured relative to P₃'s own position.
From the first equation, a₃ = −a₁. Put this into the second equation.
Put a₄ = −3a₁ into the third equation and solve for a₂.
steps.why_this_step: Each extra movable pulley in the chain multiplies the effect on the far end, which is why block 2's acceleration comes out seven times point 1's.

final_answer.value: a₂ = −7a₁ (block 2's acceleration is 7 times point 1's acceleration, in the opposite direction)

common_mistakes.text: Treating the chain of movable pulleys as a single ordinary pulley and taking a₂ = a₁ instead of a₂ = 7a₁.

items.question_text: In the arrangement shown, block A has mass 4 kg and block B has mass 5 kg. Find the acceleration of each block.
items.figure_description: A pulley P₁ is fixed to the ceiling. A single light string passes over P₁: its right end hangs straight down to block A (4 kg). Its left end goes down, passes UNDER a small movable pulley P₂ (wrapping round its lower half) and comes back up to be tied to the fixed support of P₁, so P₂ hangs in a loop of that string with two vertical strands above it. Block B (5 kg) hangs directly from the axle of P₂ by a short string. Pulleys and strings are light and frictionless. When B moves down by x, A moves up by 2x.

solution.approach: A hangs from one strand; the movable pulley (holding B) has two strands, so aA = 2aB, opposite in direction; apply Newton's second law to each block.

steps.text: Take downward as positive for each block separately. The movable-pulley string constraint gives aA = −2aB.
Write Newton's second law for A (4 kg), held by a single strand of tension T.
Write Newton's second law for B (5 kg), held by two strands of tension T at the movable pulley.
Solve the three equations together.
aA is positive, so A accelerates downward at 20/7 m/s²; aB is negative, so B accelerates upward at 10/7 m/s², half the magnitude of aA, as the constraint requires.
steps.equation: A: 20/7 m/s² ≈ 2.9 m/s² down, B: 10/7 m/s² ≈ 1.4 m/s² up

final_answer.value: A (4 kg) accelerates at 20/7 m/s² ≈ 2.9 m/s² downward, and B (5 kg) accelerates at 10/7 m/s² ≈ 1.4 m/s² upward.

common_mistakes.text: Treating both blocks as hanging from a single strand of the same tension and using the plain Atwood formula (g(mA−mB)/(mA+mB)), which ignores the movable pulley.
Using only one strand of tension in the 5 kg block's equation instead of two, giving the wrong magnitude for both accelerations.

items.question_text: In the setup shown, block m₁ rests on the sloped face of a frictionless wedge, while a second block, m₂, hangs in the air and is η times as heavy as m₁; the wedge's slope makes an angle θ with the ground. Every pulley and every string in the system is taken to be massless, and no surface exposes any friction. Work out the acceleration of block m₂.
items.figure_description: A wedge rests on the ground. Its sloped face rises from the lower-left corner, where it makes angle θ with the ground, up to the top-right corner of the wedge; its right face is vertical. A small pulley is fixed at the top-right corner of the wedge. Block m₁ rests on the sloped face. A cord is tied to block m₁, runs up the slope parallel to the incline, passes over the top of the fixed corner pulley, and drops vertically down just outside the vertical face to the axle of a second, smaller pulley. This second pulley is not fixed to anything; it hangs in the air beside the vertical face, held up only by that cord. A second cord passes over the top of this hanging pulley, and both of its segments run downward: the left segment goes straight down to a small bracket fixed to the wedge at the foot of the vertical face, at ground level; the right segment goes straight down to block m₂, which hangs freely in the air to the right of the wedge. Block m₂ has mass η times m₁. All pulleys and cords are massless, and every surface is frictionless.

solution.approach: Get the string-length constraint linking m1's motion up the incline to m2's fall, then combine it with Newton's second law for m1, the movable pulley, and m2.

steps.text: The cord from m1 goes over the fixed corner pulley down to the movable pulley; the second cord loops under the movable pulley with one end fixed and one end on m2.
steps.equation: cord 1: m1 to fixed pulley to movable pulley; cord 2: fixed bracket to movable pulley to m2

steps.text: If m1 moves a distance x up the incline, the movable pulley must move down by x (cord 1 is fixed length), and then both segments of cord 2 shorten or lengthen by that same x, so m2 must move down by 2x.
steps.why_this_step: This is the constraint relation: it links every acceleration in the system before any force equation is written.

steps.text: The movable pulley is massless, so the two upward pulls from cord 2 must together balance the one downward pull from cord 1.
Write Newton's second law for m1 along the frictionless incline, taking up the slope as positive.
steps.equation: T1 − m1 g sinθ = m1 a1

steps.text: Write Newton's second law for m2, taking downward as positive.
Substitute T1 = 2T2 and m2 = ηm1 into both equations and eliminate T2 to solve for a1.
steps.equation: T2 = ηm1(g − 2a1); T1 = m1(a1 + g sinθ) = 2T2 gives a1(1 + 4η) = g(2η − sinθ)

steps.text: So a1 = g(2η − sinθ)/(1 + 4η), and m2's acceleration is twice that.

final_answer.value: a2 = 2g(2η − sinθ)/(1 + 4η), directed downward (the acceleration of the mass m2 = ηm1)

common_mistakes.text: Missing the movable-pulley factor of 2 in the constraint and taking a2 = a1, which gives a1(1 + 2η) = g(2η − sinθ), the wrong denominator (1 + 2η) instead of (1 + 4η).

items.question_text:
A block of mass m rests on an inclined plane. For the surface of this incline, the angle of repose is 45°. Work out the friction force on the block, the net force acting on it, and its acceleration, when the incline's angle θ is set to (a) 30°, (b) 45°, and (c) 60°.
(a) Find the friction force, the net force, and the acceleration of the block when θ = 30°.
(b) Find the friction force, the net force, and the acceleration of the block when θ = 45°.
(c) Find the friction force, the net force, and the acceleration of the block when θ = 60°.
items.figure_description: A block of mass m sits on the sloped surface of an inclined plane that rises from a horizontal base; the incline makes an angle θ with the horizontal, measured at the base of the slope. The angle of repose of this surface is 45°, and θ is then set to 30°, 45°, and 60° in turn.

solution.approach: Compare each angle to the 45° angle of repose, where μ = tan45° = 1, to decide if the block stays still or slides, then apply the matching friction law.

steps.text: The angle of repose is 45°, so the coefficient of friction equals tan45°.
For θ = 30°, which is less than the angle of repose, the block stays at rest: static friction exactly balances the weight component along the incline.
steps.equation: friction = mg sin30° = 0.5mg up the incline; net force = 0; a = 0

steps.text: For θ = 45°, equal to the angle of repose, the block is on the verge of sliding but still stays at rest.
steps.equation: friction = mg sin45° = mg/√2 ≈ 0.707mg up the incline; net force = 0; a = 0

steps.text: For θ = 60°, greater than the angle of repose, the block slides down, so kinetic friction now acts up the incline.
steps.equation: friction = μmg cos60° = 0.5mg up the incline

steps.text: Find the net force and acceleration for θ = 60° from the weight component along the incline minus the kinetic friction.
steps.equation: net force = mg sin60° − 0.5mg = mg(√3−1)/2 ≈ 0.366mg down the incline; a = g(√3−1)/2 ≈ 3.66 m/s² down the incline (using g = 10 m/s²)

final_answer.value: (a) θ=30°: friction = 0.5mg up the incline, net force = 0, a = 0. (b) θ=45°: friction ≈ 0.707mg up the incline, net force = 0, a = 0. (c) θ=60°: friction = 0.5mg up the incline, net force ≈ 0.366mg down the incline, a ≈ 3.66 m/s² down the incline

common_mistakes.text: Applying kinetic friction at θ = 30°, below the angle of repose, gives a negative net force of size 0.366mg (3.66 m/s² with g = 10), showing the block cannot actually be sliding there.

items.question_text: A block of mass m rests on a horizontal, rough surface whose angle of friction is φ. Someone pulls the block using a force F directed at an angle θ above the horizontal. What is the smallest value F can take and still move the block?

solution.approach: Write the horizontal and vertical force balance for the block at the point motion begins, then rewrite the result using the angle of friction instead of the coefficient of friction.

steps.text: The pull F at angle θ has a horizontal part that drives the block forward and a vertical part that lifts it slightly, reducing the normal force from the surface.
At the point the block starts to move, the horizontal pull equals the maximum friction, which is the coefficient of friction times the normal force.
steps.equation: F cosθ = μN = μ(mg − F sinθ)

steps.text: Collect the F terms and solve for F.
steps.equation: F(cosθ + μ sinθ) = μmg ⇒ F = μmg/(cosθ + μ sinθ)

steps.text: Replace μ with tanφ, since the angle of friction φ is defined by tanφ = μ, and simplify using the cosine addition formula.
steps.equation: F = mg sinφ/(cosθ cosφ + sinθ sinφ) = mg sinφ / cos(θ − φ)

common_mistakes.text: Minimising over the pull angle as well, which gives the overall least pull mg sinφ (reached only at θ = φ), when the question fixes θ and asks for the least F at that angle.
Swapping sinφ and cosφ in the numerator gives mg cosφ / cos(θ − φ).

items.question_text: Four forces F₁, F₂, F₃ and F₄ act at a single point O, as drawn in a force diagram. Write the x-component and the y-component of each of the four forces, measured along the ox and oy axes shown in the figure.
items.figure_description: Four force vectors are drawn from a common point O. A horizontal reference line runs through O; ox points to the right along it and oy points straight up. F₁ = 4 N points up and to the right, at 30° above the +x direction. F₂ = 4 N points up and to the left, at 60° above the −x direction (the 60° is measured from the leftward horizontal, so F₂ is 30° from the +y direction). F₄ = 4 N points horizontally to the right, along +x. F₃ = 6 N points straight down along −y.

solution.approach: Resolve each force along ox and oy using the angle it makes with the axes shown in the figure.

steps.text: F₁ = 4 N is at 30° above ox, so resolve it along ox and oy.
F₂ = 4 N is at 60° above the −ox direction (30° from oy), so its ox-component is negative and its oy-component is positive.
F₃ = 6 N points straight down along −oy, so it has no ox-component.
F₄ = 4 N points along +ox, so it has no oy-component.
Collect all four results as the final set of components.

common_mistakes.text: Measuring F₂'s 60° from oy instead of from the −ox direction, giving F₂ₓ = −4sin60° = −2√3 N and F₂ᵧ = 4cos60° = 2 N instead of the correct −2 N and 2√3 N.
Giving F₃ a positive oy-component instead of negative, missing that the arrow points downward.

items.question_text: To push a body up a rough incline right at the point where it just starts to move takes exactly twice the force that would just stop that same body from sliding down the incline. Given the friction coefficient μ between body and incline, and θ as the incline's angle with the horizontal, what is tan θ in terms of μ?

solution.approach: Write the force needed to push the block up the incline and the force needed to barely hold it from sliding down, then use the given ratio between them.

steps.text: To push the block up, gravity's pull down the incline and friction (which now opposes the upward push) both work against the applied force.
To barely stop the block sliding down, friction acts up the incline at its full value and helps hold the block, so the needed applied force is smaller.
Use the given condition that F_up is twice F_hold, then divide through by mg cosθ and solve for tanθ.

common_mistakes.text: Leaving friction out of F_hold, treating it as mg sinθ alone, gives sinθ + μcosθ = 2sinθ, so tanθ = μ.
Leaving friction out of F_up, treating it as mg sinθ alone, gives sinθ = 2(sinθ − μcosθ), so tanθ = 2μ.

items.question_text: A man of mass m stands on a platform that also has mass m. He holds two ropes, each of which passes over a pulley fixed to the ceiling and then attaches to the platform he is standing on, as shown in the figure. He pulls down on each rope with a force equal to half of his own weight. What is the resulting upward acceleration of the man (and platform)?
items.figure_description: A rigid bar fixed to the ceiling holds four pulleys in a row. The man stands in the middle of a platform, both hands raised overhead to hold the two innermost ropes. On each side, one rope starts tied to an edge of the platform, runs upward and passes over the outer pulley on that side, runs horizontally along the ceiling to the neighboring inner pulley, then runs back down to the man's hand on that side. So each of the man's two hands pulls one continuous rope whose other end is fixed to the platform he stands on.

solution.approach: Each rope carries one tension throughout its length; add the upward pull on the platform and on the man's hands, then compare it to their total weight.

steps.text: Each rope has one tension throughout, equal to the force the man pulls with, which is half his weight.
Two ropes each pull up on the platform at one end and up on the man's hands at the other end, giving four upward pulls of size T in total.
The total weight of the man and the platform together is also 2mg.
The upward pull equals the total weight, so the net force, and the acceleration, is zero.

common_mistakes.text: Counting all four upward pulls, 2mg, but comparing them to the man's own weight mg alone, forgetting the platform's mass, gives a net force mg on mass m and an acceleration of g.

items.question_text: A box car begins at rest (v = 0) and holds a steady acceleration of 5 m/s² along its own line of travel, î (take g = 10 m/s²). Across the car's rough floor, a 2 kg object is given an initial push of 10 m/s along this same î direction; the coefficient of sliding (kinetic) friction between the object and the floor is 0.3, while their coefficient of static friction is known to be above 0.5. Work out how the object moves relative to the car.

solution.approach: While the object slides relative to the car, kinetic friction decelerates it; find when its velocity matches the car's, then check that static friction can then keep them moving together.

steps.text: While there is relative sliding, kinetic friction acts on the object, opposing the sliding. Its ground-frame deceleration follows from this friction alone.
Write the velocities of the object and the car and set them equal to find when the sliding stops.
Solve for the time and the common speed reached.
Check whether static friction can then keep the object moving with the car, which needs a force equal to ma_car; compare this to the maximum static friction available.

Since μₛ is given greater than 0.5, static friction is enough, so after t = 1.25 s the object moves with the car with no further sliding, having drifted 6.25 m forward relative to the car during the sliding phase.

final_answer.value: the object slides forward relative to the car for 1.25 s, drifting 6.25 m forward relative to it, reaches the car's speed of 6.25 m/s, and then moves with the car with no further relative sliding

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object slides backward relative to the car once the speeds match, since the car keeps accelerating, and missing that static friction is strong enough to hold it with the car.
Using μₛ instead of μₖ to find the initial deceleration during the sliding phase gives the wrong deceleration, since kinetic friction (not static) governs while there is relative motion.

items.question_text:
Inside a box car that starts from rest (v = 0) and keeps a steady acceleration of 5 m/s² along î, its own forward direction (take g = 10 m/s²), a 2 kg object is released on the car's flat, frictionless floor. At that instant the object already carries a sideways speed of 10 m/s along k̂, the horizontal direction at right angles to î in the floor plane (ĵ stays vertical, pointing up).
(a) Explain what path the object follows as seen by a passenger riding inside the car.
(b) Explain what path the object follows as seen by an observer standing on the ground outside.
items.figure_description: A rectangular car body sits on wheels on the ground. Inside it, three axes are drawn from a point: î points horizontally in the direction the car speeds up (forward), ĵ points straight up, and k̂ points horizontally out of that vertical plane, at right angles to î (sideways to the car's motion). Outside the car, an arrow marked a = 5 m/s² î shows its acceleration, and v = 0 marks its starting speed.

solution.approach: In the ground frame the frictionless floor exerts no force, so the object travels straight; the car's own acceleration bends this into a curved path relative to the car.

steps.text: In the ground frame, the frictionless floor gives the object no horizontal force in any direction, so it keeps its initial transverse velocity forever, moving in a straight line at constant speed.
steps.equation: ground frame: straight line at constant 10 m/s along k̂, no motion along î

steps.text: In the car's frame, the object starts with zero velocity along î (the car's direction of travel) but still feels the backward pseudo force from the car's forward acceleration, so its position along î grows backward starting from rest.
Along k̂, the car's acceleration does not affect the object's transverse motion, so it still moves at constant velocity in that direction relative to the car.
Combining these, the car's frame sees the object trace a parabola, curving backward relative to the car's forward direction as it moves along k̂.

final_answer.value: (a) in the car's frame the object traces a parabola, curving backward along î while moving at constant speed along k̂; (b) in the ground frame the object moves in a straight line at constant 10 m/s along k̂

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the object shares the car's acceleration along î in the ground frame gives a curved (parabolic) path in the ground frame, but the frictionless floor exerts no horizontal force on the object at all.

Describing the car frame motion as a straight line instead of a parabola misses that the pseudo force acts along î while the object's initial velocity is along k̂, a genuine two-dimensional combination.

items.question_text:
A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor, and a horizontal force F = 2t newtons (t in seconds) is applied to it, with g = 10 m/s². The floor gives two separate friction coefficients: static μₛ = 0.6 and kinetic μₖ = 0.4.
(a) Sketch how the block's acceleration changes with time.
(b) Work out the friction force on the block at t = 2 s and at t = 8 s.

solution.approach: Find the time when the applied force reaches the maximum static friction, then use kinetic friction for the sliding phase after that time.

steps.text: Find the maximum static friction and the time at which the applied force reaches it.
steps.equation: f(max static) = μₛmg = 0.6×2×10 = 12 N; F = 2t = 12 N at t = 6 s

steps.text: For t < 6 s the block stays still, so friction equals the applied force.
For t > 6 s the block slides, so kinetic friction takes its constant value and the net force gives the acceleration.
At t = 2 s the block is still in the static phase.
At t = 8 s the block is in the sliding phase.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 0 for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6 s, then a = t − 4 for t > 6 s, a straight line starting at (6 s, 2 m/s²) with slope 1; (b) friction = 4 N at t = 2 s, friction = 8 N at t = 8 s

common_mistakes.text: Using the static coefficient 0.6 instead of the kinetic coefficient 0.4 for the sliding phase gives friction = 12 N at t = 8 s and a = 2 m/s² instead of 4 m/s².
Forgetting to divide the net force by the mass gives a = 2t − 8 directly, so a = 8 m/s² at t = 8 s instead of the correct 4 m/s².

items.question_text:
Lined up in contact with each other on a smooth horizontal surface, from left to right, are three blocks: a 1 kg block, a 4 kg block, and a 2 kg block. A 120 N push acts on the 1 kg block from its left side, directed rightward into the row. A 50 N push acts on the 2 kg block from its right side, directed leftward into the row.
(a) Find the acceleration of the three-block system.
(b) Find the size of the normal contact force between the 1 kg block and the 4 kg block.
(c) Find the net force acting on the 2 kg block.
items.figure_description: On a smooth horizontal surface, three blocks touch each other in a row: 1 kg on the left, 4 kg in the middle, 2 kg on the right. A horizontal force of 120 N is applied to the outer (left) face of the 1 kg block, pointing right, into the row. A horizontal force of 50 N is applied to the outer (right) face of the 2 kg block, pointing left, into the row.

solution.approach: Treat all three blocks as one system to find the common acceleration, then isolate one block at a time using Newton's second law.

steps.text: Find the net external force and total mass of the system.
The system acceleration is the net force divided by the total mass.
steps.equation: a = 70/7 = 10 m/s², rightward, in the direction of the 120 N force

steps.text: Isolate the 1 kg block: the 120 N force acts forward, and the 4 kg block pushes back on it with the contact normal force N.
steps.why_this_step: The 1 kg block only touches the 120 N force and the 4 kg block, so its own equation isolates N directly.

steps.text: The net force on the 2 kg block equals its mass times the common acceleration.

final_answer.value: (a) a = 10 m/s²; (b) N = 110 N; (c) net force on the 2 kg block = 20 N

common_mistakes.text: Adding 120 N and 50 N instead of subtracting, since both forces push toward the middle of the row, giving a = 170/7 ≈ 24.3 m/s².
Using the far side (4 kg + 2 kg) but forgetting the 50 N force acting there, giving N = 6×10 = 60 N instead of 110 N.

items.question_text:
A vertical chain, from top to bottom, consists of a 5 kg block, then a uniform rope of mass 4 kg, then a 7 kg block, with the rope connecting the two blocks. An upward force F of 200 N is applied at the very top of the 5 kg block. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², answer the following.
(a) Find the acceleration of the system.
(b) Find the tension at the top of the rope.
(c) Find the tension at the mid-point of the rope.
items.figure_description: From top to bottom in a vertical line: an upward force F = 200 N pulls a 5 kg block; a uniform rope of mass 4 kg hangs below the 5 kg block; a 7 kg block hangs at the bottom of the rope.

solution.approach: Find the acceleration of the whole chain from the net upward force, then cut the rope at each point and apply Newton's second law to everything hanging below that cut.

steps.text: The total mass of the top block, rope and bottom block is 16 kg. Apply Newton's second law to the whole system under the applied force and total weight.
Compute the acceleration.
For the tension at the top of the rope, apply Newton's second law to everything below that point: the rope plus the 7 kg block, total 11 kg.
Compute this tension.
For the tension at the mid-point of the rope, the hanging mass below that cut is the 7 kg block plus half the rope's mass.

common_mistakes.text: Using g alone instead of g + a for the tension cuts gives 107.8 N and 88.2 N, ignoring the system's own acceleration.
Forgetting to include half the rope's mass below the mid-point gives 7 × 12.5 = 87.5 N there instead of 112.5 N.

concept_tags: tension in a rope with distributed mass

items.question_text: In the same pulley system, at one instant blocks 1 and 2 are each moving upward at a speed of 1 m/s. Determine the velocity of block 3 at this same instant.
items.figure_description: A fixed pulley is mounted at the top, attached to a rigid support. A string runs over this fixed pulley: block 1 hangs from one end (the left side), and the other end connects to the axle of a second, movable pulley that hangs below it. A second string runs over this movable pulley, with block 2 hanging from its left end and block 3 hanging from its right end.

solution.approach: Use the string-length constraint twice, once at the fixed pulley and once at the movable pulley, to relate the three velocities.

steps.text: Take downward as positive for every velocity. Block 1 moves upward at 1 m/s, so its downward velocity is −1 m/s.
The fixed-pulley string constraint makes the movable pulley's downward velocity the negative of block 1's downward velocity.

Block 2 moves upward at 1 m/s, so its downward velocity is −1 m/s. The movable-pulley constraint makes the sum of the downward velocities of blocks 2 and 3 equal to twice the pulley's downward velocity.
Substitute the known values and solve for v₃.

common_mistakes.text: Taking the movable pulley's downward velocity equal to block 1's downward velocity, instead of its negative, gives v₃ = 1 m/s upward instead of 3 m/s downward.

items.question_text: Inside a train carriage a 1 kg plumb bob hangs on a string from the ceiling. The train is climbing a slope of 30° at constant velocity. Take g = 10 m/s². Through what angle is the string tilted away from the normal to the ceiling, and what tension does it carry?

solution.approach: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so no pseudo force acts on the bob and it hangs exactly vertical under gravity and tension alone.

steps.text: The train moves at constant velocity, so its acceleration is zero and no pseudo force acts on the bob in the train's frame.
With no horizontal force, the string hangs vertically downward, and the tension balances the bob's weight.
The ceiling is parallel to the 30° incline, so the normal to the ceiling is tilted 30° away from the true vertical.
steps.equation: normal to ceiling is 30° from vertical

steps.text: Since the string is exactly vertical, the angle between the string and the normal to the ceiling equals the incline angle.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the string must hang perpendicular to the tilted floor (aligned with the incline's normal) gives an angle of 0°, ignoring that constant velocity means no pseudo force at all.
Adding a pseudo force along the slope even though velocity is constant tilts the string from vertical and changes the tension; with zero acceleration there is none, so T = 10 N.

items.question_text: A weight of 10 N is to be split into two components: one directed parallel to a slope, and one directed perpendicular to it. The slope makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Find both components.
items.figure_description: An inclined slope rising to the right at 30° to the horizontal ground. A weight w = 10 N acts vertically downward at a point on the slope. It is split into w∥, directed along the slope surface toward its lower end, and w⊥, directed into the slope surface, perpendicular to it. The angle between the vertical weight and the perpendicular component is 30°, and the angle between the slope surface and the vertical is 60°.

solution.approach: Split the weight into a component along the slope and a component into the slope using the incline angle.

steps.text: The weight acts vertically downward. The angle between the weight and the perpendicular to the slope equals the slope angle, 30°.
The component along the slope (parallel to the surface) is the weight times the sine of the slope angle.
steps.equation: w∥ = w sin θ = 10 × sin 30° = 5 N

steps.text: The component into the slope (perpendicular to the surface) is the weight times the cosine of the slope angle.
steps.equation: w⊥ = w cos θ = 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 N
steps.why_this_step: The 30 deg angle lies between the weight and its perpendicular component, so the perpendicular component is the adjacent side, w cos30, and the along-slope component is the opposite side, w sin30.

final_answer.value: component parallel to the slope = 5 N (down the slope); component perpendicular to the slope = 8.66 N (into the slope)

common_mistakes.text: Swapping sine and cosine gives 8.66 N along the slope and 5 N perpendicular to it.

items.question_text:
A system of three blocks — 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg — is connected by pulleys as shown in the figure and let go from rest.
(a) Work out how fast each block speeds up.
(b) Work out the pulling force carried by each string.
items.figure_description: A fixed pulley is mounted on the ceiling. A string over this fixed pulley carries tension 2T: one end holds a 1 kg block; the other end supports a second, massless, movable pulley. A separate string, carrying tension T, passes over this movable pulley: one end holds a 2 kg block and the other end holds a 3 kg block. The whole arrangement starts at rest and is then released.

solution.approach: Write Newton's second law for each of the three blocks, use the massless movable pulley to fix the tension ratio, then use the string-length constraint to link the three accelerations.

steps.text: The string over the fixed pulley has tension 2T throughout; taking downward as positive, for the 1 kg block gravity acts down and 2T acts up.
The string over the movable pulley P has tension T on each side, since pulley P is massless the string tied to its axle must carry exactly 2T to balance the two T's pulling down on it.
For the 2 kg and 3 kg blocks, gravity acts down and T acts up on each.
The main string's constant length links block 1's motion to pulley P's motion; the secondary string's constant length (measured from P) links blocks 2 and 3 to P.
Write a₂ and a₃ in terms of T from the block equations, add them, and set the sum equal to −2a₁ = −2(10−2T).
Collect terms and solve for T.
steps.why_this_step: This is the only tension value consistent with all three blocks' equations and the pulley's string constraint together.

steps.text: Put T back to get every acceleration.
steps.equation: a₁ = 10−2T = −6.55 m/s² (i.e. 6.55 m/s² upward), a₂ = 5.86 m/s² down, a₃ = 7.24 m/s² down

final_answer.value: T = 8.28 N (2T = 16.55 N); the 1 kg block accelerates upward at 6.55 m/s²; the 2 kg block accelerates downward at 5.86 m/s²; the 3 kg block accelerates downward at 7.24 m/s².
